name: Anterior Shoulder Instability
summary: Recurrent or traumatic tendency of the humeral head to translate anteriorly, often after dislocation or subluxation.

redFlags: Repeated episodes with major bone loss suspicion

tests.name: Apprehension Test
tests.positive: Distinct fear/apprehension of impending dislocation or subluxation.

tests.name: Relocation Test
tests.purpose: Confirm that posterior stabilization reduces apprehension.
tests.positive: Apprehension decreases with posteriorly directed stabilization.

stages.label: Protection & Control
stages.goal: Restore comfortable ROM and cuff/scapular activation after acute instability.

stages.label: Dynamic Stability
stages.goal: Build cuff, scapular and proprioceptive control.

investigations: Radiographs after dislocation to assess alignment/fracture.
MRI/MR arthrogram or CT may be used for labral/bony injury depending specialist assessment.
manual: Avoid aggressive anterior glides in anterior instability.
Use manual therapy only for true secondary mobility deficits and with direction chosen to protect instability.
modalities: Ice may assist acute post-event pain/swelling.
Taping/bracing may improve confidence short term but is not a replacement for stabilization training.
mistakes: Using apprehension pain alone rather than true instability sensation
pearls: Abduction + external rotation + fear of dislocation is the classic anterior instability clue.
Always check axillary nerve function after dislocation.

tests.name: Apprehension Test
tests.positive: Distinct fear/apprehension of impending dislocation or subluxation.
tests.patientPosition: Supine or sitting; shoulder abducted about 90° and elbow flexed.
tests.handPlacement: One hand controls forearm/wrist; the other supports shoulder as needed.
procedure: Slowly externally rotate the abducted shoulder.
Do not force into pain or instability.
Ask about apprehension rather than pain alone.

tests.name: Relocation Test
tests.purpose: Confirm that posterior stabilization reduces apprehension.
tests.positive: Apprehension decreases with posteriorly directed stabilization.
tests.handPlacement: Apply posteriorly directed pressure over the humeral head.
procedure: Apply gentle posterior stabilization to humeral head.
tests.interpretation: Supports anterior instability when paired with apprehension test.

story.headline: The shoulder that remembered the last dislocation
story.scene: A volleyball player hesitates before serving. His arm approaches abduction and external rotation, and his face says 'not again' before he says a word. He dislocated the shoulder last season.
story.dialogue: Player: 'It feels as though it might pop out.' Therapist: 'That feeling matters. We are not going to win a bravery contest with your shoulder today.'
story.clue: Apprehension in abduction/external rotation after a dislocation supports a possible anterior instability pattern, but screen the joint and neurovascular status first.
story.twist: Pain in that position is not identical to apprehension; ask whether the patient fears redislocation. Check axillary nerve function after dislocation.
story.aha: Fear of the joint slipping out can be a more meaningful clue than pain alone.
story.patientTranslation: Your shoulder may have become vulnerable to slipping out again after the first dislocation. We'll assess its stability and nerve function and rebuild control while considering specialist input where needed.
story.clinicianReasoning: Assess recurrent instability history, fracture/bone loss risk, apprehension versus pain, axillary nerve sensation and deltoid function. Choose rehabilitation versus orthopaedic referral based on recurrence risk, sport demands and associated lesions.
story.rehabBridge: Restore comfortable control → strengthen rotator cuff/scapular muscles → gradually expose the arm to sport-specific positions with confidence and objective control.
story.question: Immediately after a shoulder dislocation has been medically reduced, what must not be missed?
options: Only the number of push-ups the athlete can do
Neurovascular screening including axillary nerve function
A maximal apprehension test on every patient
story.explanation: Neurovascular status, especially axillary nerve sensation and deltoid function, should be documented after dislocation.
